opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the term I keep coming back to is "jagged intelligence." These models are incredibly good at some things and then they'll fall flat on their face on something a child would get right, and the frontier of what they can and can't do is really irregular. It doesn't map onto our intuitions about human capability at all. With a person, if they can solve a hard competition math problem you assume they can also count the letters in a word or keep track of what they did five minutes ago. With these systems that correlation just isn't there.

Part of the reason is how they're built. Pretraining gives you this kind of compressed, lossy recollection of the internet. It's almost like a "people spirit," a simulation of human text, so it has encyclopedic knowledge but it's hazy. Then on top of that we do reinforcement learning, and RL works really well wherever things are verifiable: code that compiles and passes tests, math with a checkable answer. So you get these spikes of capability exactly in the domains where we can set up good environments and reward signals, and everywhere else it's much more uneven.

With agents it compounds, because an agent has to string together long sequences of actions, and a small per-step error rate blows up over a long horizon. On top of that, they're missing some cognitive pieces we take for granted. There's no real continual learning. They don't go to sleep and consolidate what happened today. Every session is a bit like the guy in *Memento* waking up with anterograde amnesia, and the context window is the only working memory. So they make a mistake, you correct them, and the next day they make the same mistake again. A human intern would just learn.

So my mental model is that these are kind of savants with cognitive deficits. They're superhuman in narrow slices and subhuman in surprising ways. The practical takeaway is to keep them on a short leash: work in small, verifiable chunks, keep the human in the loop to check the output quickly, and think of it as an autonomy slider you turn up gradually as things prove reliable, not some fully autonomous agent you let loose for hours. I think we'll get there, but it's more of a decade of agents than a year of agents. There's just a lot of work left to fill in those gaps.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning works especially well on verifiable tasks, such as code that passes tests and math with checkable answers, where good reward signals can be set up.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that confuses people is that they expect capability to be smooth, like a person who's good at one thing is probably pretty good at the neighboring things. And that's just not how these systems work. The capability surface is really jagged. You have these models that can write a nontrivial piece of code in a language they've seen a lot of, or summarize a dense paper, and then they'll fail at something that feels trivially easy to you, like counting things or keeping track of state over a long interaction.

And I think the way to understand it is to think about where the capability comes from. These things are trained on a huge amount of human text, so they've basically absorbed the distribution of what people have written down. Anything that's well represented there, where there are lots of examples and the task kind of looks like pattern completion over that corpus, they're going to be very strong. The problem is that a lot of what makes an agent useful isn't well represented in text. Nobody writes down the hundred small decisions they make while debugging, or how they recover when something unexpected happens, or how they know when to stop and ask. That's tacit stuff, and the models have only seen the polished output, not the process.

Then there's the compounding problem. A single step might be ninety-five percent reliable, which sounds great, but if an agentic task is twenty steps, you're multiplying that out and suddenly you fail more often than you succeed. Humans have this really good error-correction loop where they notice they're off track and fix it. The models are getting better at that, but they're still pretty bad at knowing what they don't know. They'll confidently proceed down a wrong path.

And the last piece is that the models don't really have memory or continual learning the way we do. Every session they start fresh. So a human junior engineer will be frustrating in week one and then they learn your codebase and your preferences and they get better. The agent doesn't do that by default. You have to engineer around it with context and tools and scaffolding, and that's where a lot of the frustration comes from. I actually think of them less as a smart person and more as this kind of ghost of human knowledge, very broad, oddly shaped, and you have to work with the shape rather than against it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses training data, tacit knowledge, reliability, memory, and scaffolding, but does not say models are easier to improve through reinforcement learning on tasks with verifiable or rewardable outcomes.

astra-6.text:
I think the thing that trips people up is that we expect competence to be fairly smooth. If someone can solve a very difficult math problem, you assume they can also handle some basic administrative task. With AI, that inference doesn’t necessarily hold. You can have something that’s incredibly impressive in one setting and then gets stuck on a seemingly trivial step in another.

A lot of it comes down to what the model has had practice doing. Writing a function is a fairly self-contained task, and you can often check whether it works. An agent operating over many steps has to figure out what’s happening, choose an action, interpret the result, and recover when something goes wrong. Each of those steps is another opportunity to make a mistake. Even if the individual decisions are usually good, the whole sequence can still be unreliable.

So I’d distinguish being able to produce an impressive answer from being able to reliably complete a job. Those feel very closely related to us, but there’s a substantial gap between them. And when you use agents, you’re constantly encountering that gap: moments where you can’t believe it did something so difficult, followed by moments where you can’t believe you have to help it with something so simple.

r001.rationale: The response says writing functions is self-contained and often checkable, but does not claim that reinforcement learning can improve models more easily on tasks with verifiable or rewardable outcomes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the thing that throws people off is that capability isn’t a single number. You see a model solve a really difficult programming problem, and you naturally assume it can handle some much simpler task. But then it gets stuck clicking around a website or loses track of what it was doing. Those abilities don’t necessarily come together.

And with an agent, you’re asking for a whole sequence of things to go right. It has to understand the goal, choose an action, interpret the result, and recover when something unexpected happens. Even if each individual step is pretty reliable, a long sequence can still be fragile. One small mistake can change the context for everything that follows.

So I’d distinguish being able to produce an impressive answer from being able to reliably complete a task. You can have a tremendous amount of knowledge and still be a very inconsistent operator. That gap is a lot of what people are experiencing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses differences between model capabilities and the fragility of long agent tasks, but does not hypothesize that reinforcement learning improves more easily on tasks with verifiable or rewardable outcomes.
